title: Asia stocks tumble, S.Korea’s KOSPI slumps 7% on chip rout, Fed rate fears
full_text:
Asia stocks tumble, S.Korea’s KOSPI slumps 7% on chip rout, Fed rate fears
Investing.com -- Asian stocks tumbled on Thursday, led by South Korea’s KOSPI, as semiconductor losses deepened amid concerns over Chinese competition and hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation raised expectations for further Federal Reserve rate hikes.
KOSPI plunged 7.2%, while Japan’s Nikkei 225 sank 4.7%, extending losses across the region’s technology-heavy markets. The MSCI Asia Pacific index fell nearly 3%, putting it on course for its weakest level since July.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng fell 1.1%, while China’s CSI 300 dropped 1.4% and the Shanghai Composite lost 1.5%.
The selloff followed another weak session on Wall Street, where the the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite tumbled 1.9% overnight. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index extended its losing streak to six sessions, its longest since May 2025, while the Russell 2000 Equal Weight slipped into correction territory after falling 11% from its peak.
In Asian trade, Nasdaq 100 futures dropped 0.9% and S&P 500 futures lost 0.4%.
With Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing (TW:2330) due to report later in the day, investors are looking for a sixth consecutive quarter of record earnings and upbeat guidance to reassure markets that booming AI-chip demand can sustain growth across the semiconductor sector.
Chipmakers lead losses as AI investment faces scrutiny
South Korean memory-chip makers bore the brunt of the selloff, with SK Hynix plunging 11.2% and Samsung Electronics falling 9.4%. Japan’s Kioxia and LG Innotek lost over 10%. Taiwan’s Largan, Foxconn and TSMC fell over 2%.
The declines extended a rout triggered by concerns over Chinese semiconductor competition, after ChangXin Memory Technologies (CXMT) made progress on a higher-density DRAM design capable of storing more data.
Broadcom CEO Hock Tan’s warning that some AI investors are effectively gambling has added to concerns over stretched valuations and whether heavy infrastructure spending will deliver adequate returns.
AI financing risks have become more visible. CoreWeave shares fell as much as 17% on Wednesday, while the company’s debt due in 2032 traded below 78 cents on the dollar, compared with its original par value when investors bought the bonds four months ago.
Hong Kong and mainland China technology shares also weakened sharply. MiniMax fell 8.7%, Z.AI lost 9.1%, Semiconductor Manufacturing International Corp. dropped 4.5%, Baidu slid 4.4% and Alibaba declined 3.1%.
Hot U.S. inflation raises rate-hike risks
Hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation, driven partly by gasoline prices, strengthened the case for further Fed tightening and raised the risk of additional rate hikes to contain price pressures.
The figures have increased concerns that the Fed may need to tighten policy further even if officials had hoped to pause after September’s rate increase, which took the benchmark range to 3.75%-4.00%.
Markets raised the implied probability of a 25-basis-point hike at the Fed’s October 27-28 meeting to 31.6%, from 22.1% a day earlier, while pricing in about 40 basis points of further increases by the end of January.
Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh has said he will not guide markets through his own near-term policy outlook, but his remarks on Friday in Bangkok, during a fireside chat with International Monetary Fund Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva, will face close scrutiny.
Investors are also awaiting U.S. producer-price and retail-sales data later on Thursday.
Meanwhile, oil prices eased on Thursday, with Brent crude down $1.39 to $104.67 a barrel and U.S. West Texas Intermediate down $1.02 to $94.07.
Singapore’s Straits Times dropped 0.9% a day after the Monetary Authority of Singapore unexpectedly left monetary policy unchanged. Elsewhere, Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 and New Zealand’s NZX 50 fell 0.1%. India’s Nifty 50 Futures rose 0.4%.

title: Oil prices sink on report of easing U.S. sanctions; IEA release plans in focus
full_text:
Asia stocks tumble, S.Korea’s KOSPI slumps 7% on chip rout, Fed rate fears
Investing.com-- Oil prices fell sharply on Thursday after a report showed the U.S. considering easing sanctions on oil shadow fleets.
Focus was also on an upcoming meeting of the International Energy Agency on Thursday, which is likely to dictate the speed at which Europe will release more oil from its emergency stockpiles.
Crude was also pressured by strength in the dollar following hotter-than-expected U.S. consumer price index inflation data, which ramped up bets on more interest rate hikes.
Brent oil futures slid 1.66% to $104.31 a barrel by 23:20 ET (03:20 GMT), while West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell 1.3% to $93.86 a barrel.
Get more insights on oil markets by subscribing to InvestingPro-- with 55% off for a limited time
Oil’s losses were limited by industry data showing U.S. oil inventories shrank much more than expected in the past week amid disruptions in production along the Gulf coast.
Crude retained a bulk of its gains from earlier in the week, as renewed strikes in the Strait of Hormuz and worsening hostilities between Saudi Arabia and Yemen’s Houthis kept fears of supply disruptions in play.
Maritime officials said a container ship and a dry bulk carrier both sank in Hormuz over the past 24 hours. Separately, Yemen’s Iran-backed Houthis struck Saudi Aramco’s headquarters earlier this week.
Oil falls as U.S. considers easing oil fleet sanctions
Oil’s Thursday losses came after Reuters reported that the Donald Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on so-called shadow fleet vessels that transport oil and derivatives from sanctioned countries including Russia, Iran, and Venezuela.
The considerations come after Trump last week temporarily lifted sanctions on Russian diesel fuel exports to help offset a growing global fuel shortage.
Softer sanctions on the shadow fleet could help bring down elevated global freight rates and control oil prices. But it was not immediately clear whether the relief measures will be carried out.
Oil was also pressured by anticipation of an IEA meeting, where the agency is expected to clarify recent comments from member states regarding an additional 100 million barrel release.
IEA members had earlier this year pledged to release 400 million barrels of oil from emergency reserves, due to the U.S.-Iran war. Recently, some ministers touted an additional 100 million barrel release.
The agency, in a monthly report released on Wednesday, warned that global diesel markets could remain tight well into 2027 due ongoing crude supply disruptions and refinery outages.
But the agency also forecast overall global oil demand falling by 2.6 million barrels per day in 2026, due to pressure from higher prices.
The IEA will meet in Paris later in the day.
API data shows rise unexpected, deep draw in U.S. inventories
Elsewhere, data from the American Petroleum Institute showed U.S. oil inventories fell by 11.12 million barrels in the week to October 9, against expectations for a 1.9 million barrel build.
The surprise draw came as U.S. Gulf coast production was disrupted by Hurricane Isaias, which made landfall in the region late last week. The hurricane was seen taking nearly two-thirds of Gulf production offline.
The API data usually heralds a similar trend in official inventory data, which is due later on Thursday.

title: Australia loses 39,300  jobs unexpectedly, easing bets on another RBA rate hike
full_text:
Asia stocks tumble, S.Korea’s KOSPI slumps 7% on chip rout, Fed rate fears
Investing.com -- Australia’s employment unexpectedly fell in September, missing economists’ forecasts for an increase, while the unemployment rate rose to 4.7%, adding to signs of easing in the labour market following the Reserve Bank of Australia’s latest interest rate hike.
Employment declined by 39,300 in September, compared with economists’ expectations for a rise of 19,600 and an increase of 39,500 in August, data from the Australian Bureau of Statistics (ABS) showed on Thursday.
Get InvestingPro with AI tools at 55% off for a limited time only
The unemployment rate rose to 4.7% from 4.6% in August, exceeding expectations for it to remain unchanged. The participation rate, which measures the share of the population working or looking for work, fell to 66.8% from 67.1%, below forecasts for 67.0%.
The decline in employment was driven by a 73,700 drop in part-time jobs, which more than offset a 34,400 increase in full-time employment. The underemployment rate also rose to 6.3% from 6.2%, while the number of unemployed people increased by 8,900 to 732,000.
The figures point to a weaker labour market, although monthly employment estimates can be volatile. In trend terms, employment still increased by 15,700 in September, while the unemployment rate remained at 4.6%, the ABS said.
The data come after the RBA raised its cash rate by 25 basis points to 4.60% in late-September, its fourth increase this year, as it sought to contain persistent inflation pressures.
The latest figures could complicate the central bank’s policy outlook. A weaker employment market may help ease wage and inflation pressures over time, but the RBA has been focused on bringing inflation back under control. The RBA’s next policy meeting is scheduled for November 2-3.
The Australian dollar’s AUD/USD pair fell 0.3% and the S&P/ASX 200 index pared losses to trade 0.4% lower.

title: U.S. weighs easing sanctions on shadow fleet to curb shipping costs - Reuters
full_text:
Investing.com-- The Trump administration is considering loosening restrictions on oil tankers linked to Russia, Iran and Venezuela, seeking to ease record-high shipping costs that have disrupted global energy trade, Reuters reported on Wednesday, citing a U.S. official.
The discussions would allow sanctioned vessels to transport oil and petroleum products that are not themselves prohibited under U.S. sanctions, potentially increasing supplies moving out of the Gulf. Companies would need approval from the Treasury Department to use the vessels, the official told Reuters.
The deliberations follow President Donald Trump's temporary lifting of sanctions on Russian diesel fuel through April 7, drawing criticism from Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy and some Republican senators over concerns that the move would bolster Moscow's war funding.
Energy Secretary Chris Wright has also discussed easing restrictions to lower freight costs, according to research firm Energy Aspects, Reuters reported.
High oil and fuel prices pose a political risk for Trump ahead of the November 3 U.S. midterm elections.

title: Anthropic tells investors Q3 revenue jumped 45% to nearly $17 bln, FT reports
full_text:
Asia stocks tumble, S.Korea’s KOSPI slumps 7% on chip rout, Fed rate fears
Investing.com-- Anthropic told investors its third-quarter revenue rose sharply and that the company was profitable, the Financial Times reported on Wednesday, citing people familiar with the matter.
Anthropic’s revenue jumped nearly 50% to $16.8 billion, the FT reported, noting that the growth was slower than the blistering pace set earlier in 2026, and was also below some expectations.
The report comes as Anthropic looks to rally investors for a blockbuster initial public offering in the coming month, while fending off concerns over slowing artificial intelligence spending and profitability.
The startup gathered investors in its San Francisco office on Wednesday for a full day of presentations, the FT reported, and was seen attempting to shore up faith in its upcoming November IPO.
Anthropic told investors it was profitable on an adjusted basis in Q3, its second straight quarter of reported profitability, the FT said.
The company also told investors it was cash flow positive and was making $1.70 in revenue for every $1 spent on computing power in Q3, the report said.
But the FT noted that the company’s pace of revenue growth was slowing from earlier in the year. The company’s annualized revenue is also expected to come in below the closely watched $100 billion figure.
Anthropic is locked in a dire race with OpenAI to produce the most advanced AI models and capture a greater share of the market. But it was seen falling behind the ChatGPT creator in recent months, especially after the latter released its flagship GPT-6 Astra model.
The two are also contending with competition from significantly cheaper and nearly as powerful Chinese AI models, which present more risks to revenue.

title: IMF urges China to deploy bigger fiscal stimulus
full_text:
BANGKOK, Oct 15 (Reuters) - China must deliver bigger fiscal stimulus as its economy teeters on deflation, a senior International Monetary Fund official said on Thursday.
"We welcome the fiscal support China has provided to the economy. But in our view, it is quite limited in size and scope," Krishna Srinivasan, director of the IMF’s Asia and Pacific Department, told a press conference.
In its World Economic Outlook (WEO), the IMF projected China’s economic growth to slow to 4.5% this year from 5.0% in 2025 due to weak domestic demand. It expects growth to slow further to 4.0% in 2027.
"Most of the growth in China is explained by external demand, and so the rebalancing, which we’ve been talking about for some time, has not really materialized," Srinivasan said.
"We think that a lot more is needed in terms of fiscal stimulus in the near term until the economy reflates," he said, calling for the need to push up prices in an economy "teetering on deflation."
He also said China’s property crisis has "lingered for too long," reiterating the IMF’s proposal to take policies to rehabilitate the real estate sector such as steps to boost household confidence and build social safety nets.

title: Oil prices retreat as investors weigh supply outlook, Middle East tensions
full_text:
Asia stocks tumble, S.Korea’s KOSPI slumps 7% on chip rout, Fed rate fears
By Sam Li and Trixie Yap
Oct 15 (Reuters) - Oil prices fell more than 1% on Thursday as investors weighed risks to supply from attacks on shipping through the Strait of Hormuz against US efforts to cut petroleum shipping costs by easing sanctions on vessels.
Brent crude futures fell $1.64, or 1.6%, to $104.42 a barrel by 0337 GMT, while US West Texas Intermediate crude futures were down 98 cents, or 1%, to $94.11, reversing gains from the previous session.
WTI rose to a three-week high in the prior session after the Houthis attacked Saudi Aramco’s headquarters and Iran said it was deploying new tactics to target ships in the Strait of Hormuz and keep oil prices high.
A container ship and a dry bulk carrier both sank near the strait in the past 24 hours after being hit by projectiles in separate incidents, maritime officials said on Wednesday.
Attacks around the waterway have surged over the past 10 days, with Iran saying it is stepping up strikes in response to the US blockade of its ports and tougher sanctions introduced last month.
With the Iran war having disrupted shipping and driven up freight costs to record highs, the Trump administration is considering easing sanctions on so-called shadow-fleet vessels that have transported oil and petroleum products from countries including Russia, Iran and Venezuela to help ease prices, a US official said on Wednesday.
The new talks centre on the United States potentially allowing "legal oil" to flow on previously sanctioned vessels, the US official said.
Increased output from Russia and the Middle East has kept a lid on prices. Russia’s crude oil production rose by 65,000 barrels per day in September to 8.43 million bpd but remained down 870,000 bpd year over year, the International Energy Agency said on Wednesday.
The IEA also said crude oil exports from Middle East Gulf producers rose by 4.4 million bpd in September to around 75% of prewar levels.
"While there is little concrete evidence of a near-term peace deal, oil continues to find its way to buyers through alternative routes and logistical arrangements," said Phillip Nova’s head of market insights, Priyanka Sachdeva, in a client note.
"These workarounds have helped prevent a more severe supply shock, although they come at a higher cost and leave global flows vulnerable to further disruption."
In the US, crude oil and distillate inventories fell, while gasoline stocks rose last week, market sources said on Wednesday, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute.
Crude stocks fell by 11.1 million barrels in the week ended October 9, sources said. That was a much bigger draw than analysts polled by Reuters expected.
"Despite the sharp inventory draw, oil prices barely reacted. The failure to rise on bullish news suggests investors are cautious about chasing prices higher at current levels," said Haitong Futures in a note on Thursday.
Official numbers from the US Energy Information Administration are due at 12 p.m. EDT (1600 GMT), delayed by a day following the Columbus Day holiday on Monday.

title: AI jitters in focus; Anthropic’s reported revenue jump - what’s moving markets
full_text:
Asia stocks tumble as South Korea’s KOSPI triggers circuit breaker in tech rout
Investing.com - S&P and Nasdaq futures point lower following a drop in shares in the previous session sparked by jitters around the artificial intelligence trade and higher-for-longer interest rates. Media reports say Anthropic unveiled a jump in third-quarter revenue to institutional investors, although the rate of change of top-line growth cooled at the AI bellwether. But AI demand remains strong, with TSMC, the world’s largest contract chipmaker, posting a new record high profit.
1. Futures subdued
U.S. stock futures hovered mostly below the flatline on Thursday. By 02:54 ET (06:54 GMT), the Dow futures contract had inched up by 27 points, or 0.1%, S&P 500 futures had dropped by 38 points, or 0.5%, and Nasdaq 100 futures had fallen by 407 points, or 1.4%.
The main averages on Wall Street retreated in the prior session. Hotter-than-anticipated September consumer price growth prompted some investors to increase their bets on a Federal Reserve rate hike later this month. This sent stocks lower and U.S. Treasury yields surging, although the selloff in bonds moderated later in the session.
Analysts suggested that the modest recovery in Treasuries was linked to traders shifting out of riskier AI names and into the perceived safety of U.S. debt. Worries abounded that climbing rates could impact a wave of debt-fueled spending propping up an AI industry already grappling with intensifying competition both domestically and abroad. Shares of AI cloud group CoreWeave were especially hard hit, sliding by more than 15%, while some of its bonds tumbled to new lows in secondary markets.
At the end of the session, both the benchmark S&P 500 and tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite had slumped to their biggest one-day decreases since July.
2. Anthropic revenue surges 45% to nearly $17 billion - reports
Despite the sharp drop in AI stocks, high-profile AI frontier lab Anthropic was pushing to maintain what has been runaway enthusiasm around the nascent technology, reportedly telling institutional investors during a meeting on Wednesday that its third-quarter revenue rose by 45% to $16.8 billion.
Anthropic, whose popular Claude chatbot has made the company a standard bearer of the wider AI industry along with rival OpenAI, previously logged revenue of $11.6 billion in the second quarter and less than $5 billion in the first quarter, according to the Wall Street Journal.
In a note, analysts at Vital Knowledge said that while such solid quarter-on-quarter growth would be celebrated "in any normal world," the rate of change is cooling, possibly raising a red flag for investors.
"[I]n the land of AI, where investors are used to parabolic figures, a slowdown in growth undercuts sentiment," the analysts wrote.
The numbers are being closely scrutinized largely because Anthropic plans to raise as much as $100 billion with a valuation of roughly $2 trillion in a potential blockbuster initial public offering, the WSJ reported. When exactly that IPO will happen remains a mystery, but Anthropic is aiming to unveil more details about its operations in IPO paperwork over the coming weeks, the WSJ said.
3. TSMC’s record profit
Despite the recent fears surrounding the outlook for AI players, demand for the technology and infrastructure underpinning it appears to have remained robust.
The latest example comes from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., or TSMC, which clocked fresh record profit of 763.06 billion New Taiwan dollars in the three months to September 30, a 69% jump from a year ago.
LSEG estimates cited by Reuters had seen the figure at NT$746.3 billion.
Revenue soared by 50% to NT$1.49 trillion. Gross margin was 66.4%, operating margin was 58.7%, and net profit margin was 51.1%, TSMC said.
The company said that it had considered setting up more facilities in the U.S., potentially in Texas, as it races to ramp up capacity to meet increasing demand.
4. U.S. producer prices ahead
On the economic calendar, a monthly reading of the U.S. producer price index could offer yet another glimpse into the state of inflation in the world’s largest economy.
Month-on-month, producer prices for final demand are seen rising by 0.6% in September, compared to 0.4% in the prior month. In the twelve months to September, PPI is tipped to come in at 5.3%, versus 5.4% previously.
On Wednesday, a separate gauge of consumer price growth from the Labor Department accelerated by more than anticipated, highlighting the effect of an energy shock linked to the Iran war. This week’s inflation data is critical, as the figures will be the most up-to-date Fed policymakers will have before the convene for a two-day meeting on October 27-28.
Beyond inflation, investors will have the chance to parse through trackers of retail sales and initial jobless claims.
5. Oil dips
Oil prices fell, as traders assessed supply risks stemming from attacks on tankers near the Strait of Hormuz and a report that the U.S. is considering easing sanctions on vessels to reduce petroleum shipping costs.
Brent oil futures slid 1.9% to $104.02 a barrel by 03:35 ET, while West Texas Intermediate crude futures fell 1.1% to $94.04 a barrel.
A container ship and dry bulk container both sank near Hormuz over the past 24 hours due to strikes from separate projectiles, according to maritime officials cited by Reuters. Strikes on vessels in the critical chokepoint have increased in recent days, exacerbating concerns over ongoing disruptions to Gulf oil flows.
Fighting between Saudi Arabia and Houthi militants in Yemen has also driven worries that the Middle East conflict could be expanding, threatening traffic through other key shipping conduits, namely the Bab el-Mandeb Strait connecting the Red Sea with the Gulf of Aden.
With energy prices rising, U.S. President Donald Trump has been mulling over easing sanctions on so-called shadow fleet vessels that transport oil and derivatives from sanctioned countries including Russia, Iran, and Venezuela.
(Reuters contributed reporting)

title: TSMC Q3 profit surges to record high on AI demand; says considering Texas fab
full_text:
Asia stocks tumble as South Korea’s KOSPI triggers circuit breaker in tech rout
Investing.com-- Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co, or TSMC, clocked a stronger-than-expected third-quarter profit on Thursday, with earnings hitting another record high on robust demand from the artificial intelligence industry.
The company said that it had considered setting up more facilities in the U.S., potentially in Texas, as it races to ramp up capacity and meet increasing demand.
The world’s largest contract chipmaker said net profit surged to T$763.06 billion ($23.55 billion) in the three months to September 30. The print jumped nearly 69% year-on-year to a record high, and was also well above Reuters/LSEG estimates of T$746.3 billion.
Revenue jumped 50% to T$1.49 trillion. Gross margin was 66.4%, operating margin was 58.7%, and net profit margin was 51.1%, TSMC said.
Capacity buildout to dent margins, TSMC looking at Texas fab
Speaking in a post-earnings webcast, CFO Wendell Huang warned of a continued deterioration in TSMC’s gross margins from the company’s attempts to increase capacity-- both at home and abroad-- to meet growing chip demand.
Gross margin dilution from the buildout is expected to be closer to 2% in 2026, Huang said, while margin dilution from its overseas facilities was expected to be higher in the coming years. He forecast an at least 0.4% drop in fourth-quarter gross margin.
He said that capital spending was expected to be "significantly higher" in the coming years, citing continued, outsized demand from AI, which required more production capacity.
Huang reiterated TSMC’s 2026 capital budget of between $60 billion and $65 billion. He declined to provide a number on just how much capacity will increase in the coming months.
"We’re working very hard to increase our capacity in the U.S.," CEO C.C. Wei said in response to an analyst question. Wei said the company had looked at U.S.-based locations outside its primary Arizona site in the U.S., including in Texas, for more facilities.
Wei said the company was still in discussions over the nature of the facilities, on whether they will be run directly by TSMC or as part of a tie-up with partners such as Elon Musk’s Terrafab.
AI-driven demand to remain very strong
Huang said TSMC revenue will be between $52.3 billion and $54.3 billion, representing a 58% year-on-year increase.
Separately, CEO C.C. Wei forecast 2026 revenue growth to be around 44% year-on-year in USD terms.
"The AI market continues to be very strong... we observe increasing AI demand, fueled by the increasing adoption of agentic AI," Wei said.
"The value of semiconductors in the global AI chain is expected to continue to increase."
Thursday’s print marked a sixth straight quarter of record profits for TSMC, and an 11th straight quarter of growth, as the chipmaker continued to reap great returns from AI-fueled demand.
The company’s advanced 2-nanometer chips accounted for 8% of total wafer revenue, while 3-nm accounted for 33% of revenue.
The company is the world’s largest contract chipmaker by production capacity, and also manufactures the most advanced chips in the market. This position saw TSMC benefit greatly from increasing global demand for advanced AI processors, with NVIDIA Corporation (NASDAQ:NVDA) being among its biggest customers.
The company is also widely regarded as a bellwether for global chip demand.
TSMC’s earnings were preceded by a strong showing from chipmaking equipment major ASML Holding NV (AS:ASML), which also flagged strong AI-fueled demand earlier this week.
Still, TSMC’s earnings come amid a deep rout in chipmaking and AI equity valuations, as the prospect of rising U.S. interest rates battered the debt-heavy sector.

title: Ukraine to resume strikes on Russian refineries, Zelenksy tells FT
full_text:
Asia stocks tumble as South Korea’s KOSPI triggers circuit breaker in tech rout
Investing.com-- Ukraine will resume attacking Russia’s oil infrastructure, President Volodymyr Zelensky said in a Financial Times interview published on Thursday.
Zelensky expressed anger at what he deemed as a “dangerous” withdrawal of U.S. intelligence earlier this week, as well as the simultaneous weakening of SpaceX’s Starlink satellite internet service.
“The block [on attacking refineries] is out. We’re done,” Zelensky told the FT, while also criticizing Washington’s eagerness for business deals with Moscow and President Donald Trump’s apparent admiration for Russia’s Vladimir Putin.
Trump had abruptly announced an “energy ceasefire” between Ukraine and Russia late last week, amid increasing pressure from Washington on Kyiv to stop hitting Russia’s refineries.
This was after Trump announced a diesel supply deal with Russia, and accused Ukraine of driving up global fuel prices.
Zelensky told the FT that Kyiv had halted attacks on Russian refineries for three days to comply with Washington’s demands, but that Moscow had continued battering Ukraine in the period.
He also said his forces had been left without early-warning alerts for Russian missile attacks, while Starlink’s satellite communications were slowed across the country, impacting frontline operations.
He dismissed the idea that the Starlink failures were a technical glitch.
Trump had earlier denied Washington had stopped sharing intelligence with Ukraine. Separately, SpaceX CEO Elon Musk said that Starshield systems– the military grade satellite network built on Starlink– was owned and controlled by the U.S. government, and that any limits on speed were ultimately decided by Washington.

title: U.S. Treasury yields slide after CPI-driven spike

Investing.com-- U.S. Treasury yields fell sharply early-Thursday, reversing course after rallying on hotter-than-expected inflation data as markets maintained bets on no interest rate hikes in October.
Heightened safe haven demand also spurred buying into Treasuries, as a widespread, deep rout in technology and artificial intelligence stocks sent investors racing for cover.
The benchmark 10-year yield fell 1.6% to 5.104% after rising as high as 5.333% on Wednesday evening.
20-year yields fell 1.3% to 5.503%, 30-year yields slid 1.3% to 5.455%, and 5-year rates fell 1.7% to 4.908%.
Yields had risen across the board on Wednesday after consumer price index inflation data read stronger than expected for September.
The print ramped up bets that the Federal Reserve will hike interest rates at least once before the end of the year. Markets are pricing in a 70.6% chance the Fed will raise rates by 25 basis points in December, CME Fedwatch showed.
But bets on an October hold remained intact, with the CPI print coming in only a smidge above market expectations.
Safe haven demand also spurred buying into bonds and brought down yields on Thursday. A wipeout in global tech and AI equities saw investors racing to safe havens like Treasuries and gold.
Bets on rising interest rates undermined prospective long-term gains from the AI trade, especially given that several major companies are heavily leveraged on debt and are sensitive to any increases in borrowing costs.
This sparked a wave of losses in tech, with the NASDAQ Composite sliding nearly 1.9% on Wednesday. South Korea’s KOSPI slid 8% and hit a lower circuit breaker on Thursday.

The dollar index fell 0.4% to 102.16 by 03:02 ET (07:02 GMT) after 0.4% gains on Wednesday following the inflation report.

Traders reassess Fed hike bets after hot U.S. CPI
U.S. consumer prices rose 3.7% year-on-year in September, accelerating from 3.4% in August and exceeding economists’ 3.6% forecast. Core consumer prices increased 2.6% annually, above expectations for 2.5%, reviving concerns that the Fed may need to tighten monetary policy further.
However, comments from Fed officials, including Vice Chair Michelle Bowman and San Francisco Fed President Mary Daly, suggested policymakers could wait for a clearer picture of inflation before tightening policy further.
Markets initially raised expectations of a rate increase at the Fed’s October 27-28 meeting after the data, but those odds subsequently eased as Treasury yields retreated and policymakers signalled caution.
Traders are currently pricing in a roughly 30% chance of a hike this month, up from 20% before the data, according to CME FedWatch.
Investors were also awaiting U.S. producer price and retail sales data, as well as remarks from Fed officials, for further clues on the policy outlook.
Yen gains on intervention warnings; Aussie slips after weak jobs report
The Japanese yen’s USD/JPY pair fell 0.3% as Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama renewed warnings against excessive currency moves.
Japan and the United States have maintained their commitment to coordinated action against disorderly currency movements following a rare joint intervention on July 31.
The Australian dollar’s AUD/USD pair fell 0.5% after domestic employment unexpectedly fell in September.
Data showed employment declined by 39,300, defying expectations for a 20,000 increase. The unemployment rate held at 4.7%, its highest in five years, while the fall was driven by a 73,700 drop in part-time jobs.
The figures reduced expectations of further monetary tightening by the Reserve Bank of Australia, with markets pricing in about a 90% chance the central bank would leave its cash rate unchanged at 4.6% in November.
Elsewhere, the Indian rupee’s USD/INR pair edged up 0.1%.

title: Analysts say UK’s August growth beat opens door to higher interest rates
full_text:
Asia stocks tumble as South Korea’s KOSPI triggers circuit breaker in tech rout
Investing.com -- Britain’s economy grew unexpectedly in August, extending a run of resilient data that will encourage finance minister John Healey as he prepares his budget against a tough financial backdrop.
The Office for National Statistics said gross domestic product rose 0.1% in August, against a consensus forecast for a 0.1% drop, after two straight 0.4% monthly gains.
Annual growth picked up to 2.1%, the strongest since October 2022, when output was rebounding from COVID-19, and the strongest since December 2019 excluding that period.
The FTSE 100 share index was up 0.33%, while the pound rose 0.39% against the dollar to $1.3244, as of 03:58 ET (07:58 GMT).
The economy was 1.8% bigger in the three months to August than a year earlier, Financial Markets Online said.
The ONS said computer programming was the largest contributor to growth over that period, and services growth was broad-based.
Manufacturing output rose 1.2% in August, defying forecasts for a small drop, and lifted industrial production 0.8%. Services were flat after a 0.5% rise in July, beating forecasts for a 0.1% dip. Construction fell 0.2%, its fourth straight decline.
Consumer-facing services fell 0.3% after a 0.1% drop in July, led by sports, amusement and recreation and restaurants.
Capital Economics said some of that could reverse earlier World Cup and hot-weather boosts, or show households cutting spending because of higher fuel and utility prices.
"The UK’s solid economic data has showered gifts on its new Chancellor but given a mixed blessing to borrowers and homeowners," said Samuel Fuller, director of Financial Markets Online.
The Bank of England is widely expected to raise its base rate to 4% in three weeks, Fuller said. With the average five-year fixed mortgage at 6%, higher rates could "slam the brakes on the already embattled property market," he said, with hundreds of thousands due to remortgage.
Paul Dales, chief UK economist at Capital Economics, said the economy was "more robust than we thought" but he still expected higher inflation to dampen growth, with businesses doing well partly on AI-related spending while households turn cautious.
Dales said that if GDP was flat in September, third-quarter growth would be 0.7%, compared with forecasts of 0.5% from Capital Economics and 0.4% from the Bank of England.
If the economy records no growth in the fourth quarter, GDP would expand 1.5% in 2026, against Capital Economics’ forecast of 1.4%. Fuller said the IMF expects the economy to grow 1.3% in 2026.
